title: Umm Ayman
hook: the woman who nursed the baby Muhammad ﷺ, whom he called my mother after my mother

segments.voice: Yesterday, Usamah ibn Zayd, the young commander the Prophet defended in public. Your line was: young and trusted. What did you hand over, and did you let it go? Day eight hundred thirty.

Two leaders of Medina walk to the house of an old woman. One is Abu Bakr, the new leader of the community. The other is Umar. The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, has died, and Abu Bakr says to Umar: come, let us visit Umm Ayman, the way the Prophet used to visit her. They knock. They sit with her. And she begins to cry. Before we hear why, it helps to know who she was, and why the Prophet kept going to her door. Today: Umm Ayman.
screen: `TWO LEADERS AT HER DOOR.` → `AS THE PROPHET USED TO VISIT.` → `SHE BEGINS TO CRY.`

segments.voice: Her name, tradition says, was Barakah. A note in Sahih Muslim, from the early scholar Ibn Shihab, describes her plainly. She came from Abyssinia, she served in the household of Muhammad's father, and after his father died she looked after the baby until he was grown. She was the mother of Usamah. Nursed here means cared for and carried, not breastfed; his milk-mothers were other women. So yesterday's young commander was her son, and Zayd was her husband. Tradition says that when Muhammad's mother died on a journey, it was Umm Ayman who brought the little boy home, and that years later he would say of her: she is my mother after my mother. That line comes from the biographies, so hold it as the tradition's memory. What Muslim records firmly is the visit. Abu Bakr and Umar come to her house after the Prophet's death. She weeps, and they try to comfort her. Don't you know, they say, that what is with God is better for His Messenger? And she answers: I know that. That is not why I am crying. I am crying because the revelation from heaven has stopped. And her answer, the report says, moved them to tears as well, and they wept with her. Look at the shape of it. The woman who carried the baby is the one who understands, before anyone says it, what has ended. The leaders came to comfort her, and she ended up teaching them. And they came because he used to come. Honoring the woman who raised him did not end with his death. It went on, through a visit.
screen: `BARAKAH, FROM ABYSSINIA.` · `SHE CARED FOR THE BABY MUHAMMAD.` · `ABU BAKR AND UMAR VISIT HER.` · `THE REVELATION HAS STOPPED.` · then, large: `MY MOTHER AFTER MY MOTHER.`

segments.voice: The practice: thank a caregiver. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone who looked after you when you were small, or when you were sick, or when you were new somewhere. A grandmother, a nanny, an aunt, a neighbor, a nurse, a teacher. Maybe not a parent. Maybe someone the world didn't call family. Breathe in, and remember one specific thing they did. Breathe out, and say thank you in your mind. If they're living, think about how you might tell them. If they've died, and you pray, you can ask mercy for them. The bell holds the time.
Umm Ayman. The woman who nursed and cared for the baby Muhammad, mother of Usamah, visited by the Prophet and, after him, by Abu Bakr and Umar. Today's word.
Your line: my mother after my mother. Today, thank one person who cared for you, with a call, a message, or a visit. Day eight hundred thirty.

howItsDone: Muslims remember Umm Ayman as the Prophet's nurse and the mother of Usamah, and retell the report in Sahih Muslim of Abu Bakr and Umar visiting her after his death.

fork.reveal: Muslim reports Abu Bakr said: let us visit Umm Ayman as the Messenger of God used to visit her. and she ended up teaching them.

original.note: Arabic: 'mother of Ayman', a name taken from her son Ayman.

trapdoor: what you thought: Umm Ayman was a minor figure in the household.
what it means: she cared for the baby Muhammad, was mother of Usamah, and was visited and honored by the Prophet, then by Abu Bakr and Umar.
what a scholar hears: Sahih Muslim's report of the visit, where her grief is not for the Prophet's fate but for the end of revelation.

sources.ref: Sahih Muslim 2454 (Abu Bakr and Umar visit Umm Ayman; she weeps that revelation has stopped)
Sahih Muslim 1771 (Ibn Shihab's note: Umm Ayman, mother of Usamah, an Abyssinian servant of Abdullah ibn Abd al-Muttalib, looked after the Prophet until he was grown)
Ibn Sa'd, al-Tabaqat al-Kubra (her name Barakah; 'my mother after my mother')

notes: Audit (serious): the teach credited Anas with the description of Umm Ayman; in Muslim 1771 that description (Abyssinian, servant of Abdullah, tahdunuhu, mother of Usamah) is Ibn Shihab's added note, so it is now attributed to him, and her Abyssinian origin and service are given as in Muslim, not as tradition. 'Nursed' (index wording) clarified as caring for, not breastfeeding (hadana; his milk-mothers were Halimah and Thuwaybah), in teach, screen, match and trapdoor. Confirm.

'My mother after my mother', her name Barakah, Abyssinian origin, and her bringing the boy home after Aminah's death are from the sira (Ibn Sa'd and others); framed as tradition. Confirm attributions.
Hadith numbers cited from memory; confirm Muslim 2454 and 1771, and the paraphrase of Anas ('nursed and cared for').
Umm Ayman's marriage to Zayd ibn Harithah is stated; confirm.
'Honoring the people who raised us is a thread that runs through the sunnah' is general; confirm.
Original: Ayman as the name of her son from an earlier marriage; confirm the note.
Editor: cut the unsourced general claim that honoring those who raised us 'runs through the sunnah'; the line now stays with this report.
